title: Make the commands work on a default Windows box, and stop headers hiding a testable gate

history.detail:
CONDITIONAL: CONDITIONAL — round 1. Audited 5f2b290 (with b0b9679, e33ec1e, 5cc1906), main checkout. Sprint file read fresh — it WAS amended mid-build (Req 5 became the version-marker requirement, the old Req 5 moved to Req 6, and Req 2 gained the clearable path I flagged last turn). Audited against the current file and the current numbering.

Neither FAIL trigger fired. Reqs 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and the first half of Req 1 are met. One requirement is not, and the reason it is not is the reason its criterion was written the way it was.

================================================================
ANSWERING YOUR QUESTION FIRST — THE REQ 3 SIMULATION MEETS THE BAR
================================================================

You asked whether the alias-toggle simulation counts or whether a from-scratch python.org install is still needed. It counts, and the criterion is the reason: "confirm this was attempted and that the outcome — established or not obtainable — is recorded plainly. **An inference from the macOS proof is a FAIL.**" The FAIL trigger is inference from macOS. You did not infer; you ran it on the real VM, produced the shape that matters (python3 unrecognized, python a real 3.13.14), exercised both a read command and a write command through the resolved interpreter, and labelled it a simulation rather than a from-scratch install. That is the outcome recorded plainly.

One thing that strengthens it further, and is worth putting on the record rather than leaving as a caveat: the untested `py` branch is unreachable in the scenario the requirement names. findPython3Interpreter resolves python3 -> python -> py in order, so `py` is only ever consulted when `python` is absent or is not Python 3. A python.org install creates both `python` and `py`, so on the very machine the requirement describes, resolution stops at `python` and `py` is never reached. "py stays untested" is therefore not a gap in the proof — it is a branch the requirement's own scenario cannot enter. Say that in the notes rather than carrying it as an open caveat; it reads as a weakness right now and it is not one.

================================================================
REQ 2 — MET, AND THE UNTESTED HALF IS COVERED BY CONSTRUCTION
================================================================

You flagged that the Python-prerequisite warning specifically was not re-triggered live. It does not need to be, and I verified why rather than accepting the reasoning:
  - Non-ASCII in non-comment code in install.js: ZERO. Checked by parsing the file and stripping
    comment text, not by grepping the whole file (which still shows 79 comment lines, all prose).
  - Real captured stdout, run twice against a scratch target — a clean install, then a run with a
    genuine CLAUDE.md conflict: 1896 and 2764 characters, ZERO non-ASCII in either. The conflict
    section is present in the second.
If the source can emit no non-ASCII byte, and ASCII is confirmed to render correctly on that console, then every message it prints is covered — including the one not separately triggered. Static plus dynamic together establish it; neither alone would. That is the right pair of tests and it is why the gap you flagged honestly is not actually a gap.

The live Windows half is the part that could not be substituted, and you did it: a genuine conflict triggered on the real VM, raw PowerShell output read, every dash a plain character. Not derived from code-page reasoning.

================================================================
REQ 1, FIRST HALF — MET
================================================================

Grepped all twelve command files rather than the three named, as the criterion instructs: zero hardcoded `/tmp` paths anywhere. The three outstanding files follow sprint 12's shipped working-directory-relative pattern rather than a second invented one. resolve_text() fails via die() naming the attempted path instead of raising.

================================================================
FINDING 1 (blocking) — REQ 1's SECOND HALF WAS REASONED, NOT RUN
================================================================

The criterion: "confirm `sprint-new.md` no longer depends on the Write tool, and that a headless Master Controller **can actually create a sprint** under the scoped profile. **If that was reasoned rather than run, it is not met** — it is the exact inference sprint 12 disproved."

There is no record of that run. I looked in the commit messages for 5cc1906..HEAD, in sprint 14's own state-file history (one event: sprint_started), and in the permission-scope findings document. Nothing. Your handoff does not claim one either — it claims the file gained the fallback, which is the change, not the demonstration.

This one is not a formality. The criterion demanded a run specifically because the analogous inference was wrong once already, and it turns out to be wrong again here — see Finding 2, which is what a run would have surfaced immediately.

================================================================
FINDING 2 (blocking) — THE NEW NOTE STATES SOMETHING THAT IS NOT TRUE
================================================================

sprint-new.md's new headless note says:

  "if the Write tool is unavailable (a headless Master Controller session under a scoped permission
   profile **never has it** — this was the second defect here: the instruction above required Write,
   and nothing else was offered, so headless Master Controller could not create a sprint at all)"

A headless Master Controller has the Write tool. Read the shipped profiles in run-role.js:
    master-controller   disallowedTools: []
    dev-team-1          disallowedTools: []
    qa1                 disallowedTools: ['Edit', 'Write']
    liveqa              disallowedTools: ['Edit', 'Write']
Only qa1 and liveqa have it removed. That is sprint 12's own deliberate design — those two roles never write source; Master Controller does, because writing sprint files is its job.

And sprint 12's findings document already recorded this by running it: "The `Write` tool, writing a file WITHIN the working directory, succeeded under plain `acceptEdits` alone — CONFIRMED, no allowlist needed." That was Master Controller's own scenario, tested directly.

So the parenthetical describes a defect that did not exist for this role. What sprint 12 actually found for Master Controller was different and narrower: `node scripts/run-lifecycle.js new` needed an explicit allowlist entry, which it has.

WHY THIS MATTERS RATHER THAN BEING A WORDING NIT: the note tells a headless Master Controller that it "never has" a tool it does have. A role reading its own command file and believing that will route around a working path — and the printf fallback, while harmless in itself, is now presented as a necessity rather than a belt-and-braces alternative. This is the fourth time in four sprints that a claim in shipped guidance has not survived checking (sprint 12's heredoc, sprint 12's /tmp destination, sprint 13's "docs/sprints never ships," this), and every one of them was a claim that a run would have settled.

REQUIRED FIX, both findings together, because they are one root cause:
  1. Run it. Launch a headless Master Controller under the scoped profile and have it create a sprint.
     That is the criterion, and it settles Finding 2 as a side effect.
  2. Correct the note to what the run establishes. If Write works for this role — and both the shipped
     profile and sprint 12's confirmed finding say it does — then the printf form is a portable
     alternative worth documenting, not a workaround for a missing tool. Keep it; describe it
     accurately.

================================================================
REQS 4, 5, 6, 7 — MET
================================================================

Req 4 — read cold against sprint 10's header, which I pulled from 3-done to compare rather than trusting the quotation. The new bullet quotes it verbatim, names the actual defect precisely (the pairing of a stated impossibility with a "record nothing" off-ramp offered in the same breath, before anyone has tried), and tells Master Controller what to write instead. Sprint 10's header fails under it unambiguously. The rule is written correctly.

Req 5 — the invariant is stated at writeInstalledVersion()'s write site and matches what the code does. It is careful in exactly the place the criterion warns about: it states what the guarantee covers (FRAMEWORK_OWNED, including scripts/launcher), what it does not (USER_OWNED tracked files, which syncTrackedUserOwnedFile can deliberately leave un-synced on an unresolved conflict without aborting), and that the read side degrades the opposite way on purpose. It also names the node_modules case, which nobody asked for and which is the one a consumer would actually get wrong. It does not promise more than the code delivers.

Req 6 — package.json 0.1.15.

Req 7 — ran everything: ALL SMOKE TESTS PASSED; ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED, 125 OK (up 2, matching the two new Req 2 tests); verify-tarball.sh TARBALL VERIFICATION PASSED, "Installed 0.1.15 (first install)".

The two new launcher tests are the right pair — a static scan for non-ASCII outside comments, and a dynamic check on real captured stdout with both a conflict and a missing-interpreter warning firing. I reproduced both independently and both hold.

================================================================
INFORMATIONAL
================================================================

1. The baseline-fixture breakage is on its fourth occurrence, root cause still unfixed. I see sprint 16 is now drafted for it ("make the baseline table maintain itself and stop tests breaking on its drift"), which is the right outcome — recording that it took four occurrences, and that I first flagged the generator drifting in sprint 9's notes, so the interval is on the record rather than in a handoff.
2. docs/sprints/registry.json is modified and uncommitted, and sprints 15 and 16 are untracked in 1-todo. Not in this diff; flagging for whoever commits next.

RECOMMENDATION

One run and one correction. The run is the requirement; the correction falls out of it. Then round 2 is short — everything else is verified and I have no other open items.

Worth saying plainly: this sprint's own Req 4 is a rule about not asserting what you have not attempted, and the one thing holding it up is an assertion that was not attempted. That is not irony worth a joke, it is the reason the rule is being written.
